lines.text: Do you know how SpaceX's rocket catch works? No landing legs. It gets grabbed out of the air by a pair of giant metal arms.
This is Super Heavy, the booster under Starship. Seventy one meters of stainless steel, with thirty three engines at the bottom.
A few minutes after launch, the ship separates and flies on. The booster flips around, relights its engines, and heads back home.
On the way down, four grid fins at the top steer it through the air, like rudders.
Near the ground, it lights thirteen engines to brake hard, then just the center three for the final, gentle hover.
Then it slides sideways, right in between two arms on the launch tower. SpaceX calls them the chopsticks.
The arms close, small pins on the booster settle onto them, and the engines shut off. Caught.
Why bother? No landing legs means less weight. And the booster comes back right where it launched, ready to fly again.
The first catch happened in October twenty twenty four. And it worked on the very first try.
So next time you watch a giant rocket come home, remember. It doesn't land. It gets caught.
Orbi Transfer dot com. Now you know!
